title: Αἴσωπος ἐν ναυπηγίῳ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 19 (= Perry 8). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Αἴσωπος ὁ λογοποιὸς σχολὴν ἄγων εἰς ναυπήγιον εἰσῆλθε.
sentences.tr: Aisōpos ho logopoios scholēn agōn eis naupēgion eisēlthe.
sentences.l: Aesop the story-maker, being at leisure, went into a shipyard.
sentences.i: Aesop the story-maker, with time on his hands, went into a shipyard.
sentences.n: σχολὴν ἄγω is the idiom “to be at leisure”; ἄγω with an abstract noun regularly does the work of “have, keep, spend”. λογοποιός is a “maker of λόγοι” — of tales; the same word can mean a prose author or a spreader of rumours. This is one of the few fables in which Aesop himself walks on as a character.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ ναυπηγῶν σκωπτόντων τε αὐτὸν καὶ ἐκκαλουμένων εἰς ἀπόκρισιν, ὁ Αἴσωπος ἔλεγε τὸ παλαιὸν χάος καὶ ὕδωρ γενέσθαι, τὸν δὲ Δία βουλόμενον καὶ τὸ τῆς γῆς στοιχεῖον ἀναδεῖξαι παραινέσαι αὐτῇ ὅπως ἐπὶ τρὶς ἐκροφήσῃ τὴν θάλασσαν.
sentences.tr: Tōn de naupēgōn skōptontōn te auton kai ekkaloumenōn eis apokrisin, ho Aisōpos elege to palaion chaos kai hydōr genesthai, ton de Dia boulomenon kai to tēs gēs stoicheion anadeixai parainesai autēi hopōs epi tris ekrophēsēi tēn thalassan.
sentences.l: And the shipwrights mocking him and calling him out to an answer, Aesop said that in old time chaos and water came to be, and that Zeus, wishing to bring to light the element of earth as well, urged her to gulp down the sea three times over.
sentences.i: The shipwrights jeered at him and challenged him to answer back, so Aesop told them that in the beginning there was chaos and water, and that Zeus, wanting to bring the element of earth to light as well, urged her to swallow the sea down three times over.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute opens the sentence, then everything after ἔλεγε goes into accusative-and-infinitive: χάος… γενέσθαι, τὸν Δία… παραινέσαι. Greek can hold a whole stretch of narrative in that construction where English says “he said that…” once and then simply keeps going. τὸ παλαιόν is an adverbial accusative, “in old times”. ἐκροφέω is to gulp or slurp down, the word used of soup. αὐτῇ is the earth, feminine in Greek and half a person here.

sentences.t: Κἀκείνη ἀρξαμένη τὸ μὲν πρῶτον τὰ ὄρη ἐξέφηνεν, ἐκ δευτέρου δὲ ἐκροφήσασα καὶ τὰ πεδία ἀπεγύμνωσεν· « ἐὰν δὲ δόξῃ αὐτῇ καὶ τὸ τρίτον ἐκπιεῖν τὸ ὕδωρ, ἄχρηστος ὑμῶν ἡ τέχνη γενήσεται. »
sentences.tr: Kakeinē arxamenē to men prōton ta orē exephēnen, ek deuterou de ekrophēsasa kai ta pedia apegymnōsen· « ean de doxēi autēi kai to triton ekpiein to hydōr, achrēstos hymōn hē technē genēsetai. »
sentences.l: And she, having begun, first brought the mountains to light, and having gulped a second time laid bare the plains as well; « but if it seems good to her to drink the water up a third time too, your craft will become useless. »
sentences.i: She set to; the first draught brought the mountains to light, and with a second gulp she laid the plains bare as well — « and if she takes it into her head to drink the water down a third time, your trade will be good for nothing. »
sentences.n: The narrative slips out of reported speech into Aesop's own words to the shipwrights, and the sting is the last clause: dry land everywhere and no use for shipbuilders. δοκεῖ μοι with the infinitive is the standard “it seems good to me to…”, i.e. “I decide to”. Κἀκείνη is καὶ ἐκείνη run together by crasis. The three swallows are counted three different ways (τὸ μὲν πρῶτον, ἐκ δευτέρου δέ, τὸ τρίτον) — Greek variety, not carelessness.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ τοὺς κρείττονας χλευάζοντες λανθάνουσι μείζονας ἑαυτοῖς τὰς ἀνίας ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐπισπώμενοι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi tous kreittonas chleuazontes lanthanousi meizonas heautois tas anias ex autōn epispōmenoi.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who mock their betters escape their own notice drawing upon themselves greater vexations from them.
sentences.i: The story shows that those who mock their betters are drawing greater troubles on themselves from those very people, and never notice they are doing it.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a supplementary participle turns English inside out: the participle carries the action and the verb reports that it went unnoticed — λανθάνουσι… ἐπισπώμενοι, “they escape notice drawing”, i.e. “they draw it on themselves without realising”. Worth recognising on sight; τυγχάνω (“happen to”) and φθάνω (“do first”) work the same way. οἱ κρείττονες, “the stronger”, is the ordinary word for one's superiors.
